title: Supply, Demand and the Price
bigQuestion: Why does the price of the same cup of lemonade go up on some days and down on others?

story.title: A Price War on Elm Street
story.kicker: Two lemonade stands, one hot Saturday, and a lesson about prices.
paragraphs: It was the hottest Saturday of June on Elm Street. Jada set up her lemonade stand at nine in the morning. Her sign said 50 cents a cup. By ten o'clock, a line of thirsty people stretched past the mailbox.

Jada sold cups as fast as she could pour them. Her pitcher ran low. People still waited in line. So Jada made a new sign. Now a cup cost 75 cents. A few people left, but most still paid. They were very thirsty.

Then Leo, who lived across the street, saw the long line. He had lemons and cups too. By noon he opened his own stand. His sign said 60 cents a cup. Half of Jada's line walked across the street to Leo.

Jada looked at her pitcher and then at Leo's sign. She changed her price to 55 cents and added a free ice cube. Leo added a paper straw. By the end of the day, both stands had sold out. The buyers got good deals, and Jada and Leo each earned money.
story.think: Why did Jada raise her price in the morning, and why did she lower it after Leo opened his stand?

lessons.title: What Is a Market?
lessons.mainIdea: A market is any place where buyers and sellers meet to trade goods or services.
reading: Picture a farmers market on a Saturday morning. Farmers bring tomatoes, corn and honey. Families walk from table to table. The farmers are sellers. The families are buyers. When they trade money for food, a *market* is working.

A *buyer* is a person who pays for a good or service. A *seller* is a person who offers a good or service for money. A market does not need a building. A lemonade stand is a market. So is a website where people buy shoes.

Every market has two sides. Buyers want to get things for a low price. Sellers want to get a high price. The price they agree on is where the trade happens. In this chapter, you will learn what pushes that price up or down.

words.d: any place or way that buyers and sellers meet to trade
a person who pays money for a good or service
a person who offers a good or service in exchange for money

look.title: Markets All Around You
look.text: A girl buys a snack from a vending machine. A family orders pizza on a phone app. A boy sells his old bike to a neighbor. A school holds a bake sale in the gym.
look.prompt: Which of these are markets? Name the buyer and the seller in each one.

check.q: Which of these is a market?
choices: A garage sale where neighbors buy old toys
A tree growing in a park
A kid reading a library book
A dog sleeping in the sun
check.why: A market is where buyers and sellers trade. At a garage sale, neighbors pay money for toys.

check.q: At a bake sale, a parent pays $1 for a cookie. Who is the seller?
choices: The people running the bake sale
check.why: The seller offers the good for money. The people running the bake sale offer the cookie.

check.q: Does a market need a building?
choices: Yes, it must be a store
Yes, it must be a mall
No, it can be a stand, a website or a yard
No, because markets have no buyers
check.why: A market is any place or way buyers and sellers meet. It can be outside or online.

lessons.title: Demand: What Buyers Want
lessons.mainIdea: Demand is how much people want to buy at each price; when the price goes down, people buy more.
reading: Leo sells cookies at school. At $2 a cookie, only 10 kids buy one. At $1, 25 kids buy one. At 50 cents, 40 kids buy one. As the price went down, more kids wanted to buy. That is demand at work.

*Demand* is how much of something people want to buy at each price. There is a pattern. When the price goes up, people buy less. When the price goes down, people buy more. This pattern is called the *law of demand*.

Why does this happen? When a cookie costs less, it is easier to afford. Some kids who said no at $2 say yes at $1. A common mistake is to think wanting is enough. Demand means wanting something and being able and willing to pay for it.

words.d: how much of a good people are willing and able to buy at each price
when the price goes up, people buy less; when the price goes down, people buy more

look.title: Leo's Cookie Demand
look.prompt: How many more cookies do kids want at $1.00 than at $2.00?

check.q: In Leo's table, how many more cookies do kids want at $1.00 than at $2.00?
check.why: At $1.00 kids want 25. At $2.00 they want 10. 25 - 10 = 15.

check.q: The price of a slice of pizza rises from $2 to $4. What does the law of demand say will happen?
check.why: The law of demand says when the price goes up, people buy less.

check.q: Mia wants a $300 bike but has no money and cannot get any. Is that demand?
choices: No, demand means being willing and able to pay
No, because bikes are not goods
check.why: Demand means wanting something and being able to pay for it. Wanting alone is not demand.

lessons.title: Supply: What Sellers Offer
lessons.mainIdea: Supply is how much sellers will offer at each price; when the price goes up, sellers offer more.
reading: Jada bakes muffins to sell. If she can get only 50 cents a muffin, she bakes 10. It is hardly worth her time. If she can get $1, she bakes 20. If she can get $2, she bakes 35 and asks her brother to help.

*Supply* is how much of something sellers will offer at each price. Supply has its own pattern. When the price goes up, sellers offer more. When the price goes down, sellers offer less. This is called the *law of supply*.

Why? A higher price means more money for each item. That makes the extra work worth it. New sellers may join in too. Notice that supply and demand go opposite ways. Buyers want more when the price is low. Sellers offer more when the price is high.

words.d: how much of a good sellers are willing and able to offer at each price
when the price goes up, sellers offer more; when the price goes down, they offer less

look.title: Jada's Muffin Supply
look.prompt: What happens to the number of muffins Jada bakes as the price goes up?

check.q: In Jada's table, how many muffins does she bake at $1.50?
check.why: Read the row for $1.50. Jada bakes 28 muffins at that price.

check.q: Farmers can now sell a bushel of corn for more money than last year. What will most farmers do?
check.why: The law of supply says sellers offer more when the price goes up.

check.q: How are the law of demand and the law of supply different?
choices: Buyers want more at low prices; sellers offer more at high prices
Both buyers and sellers want high prices
Both buyers and sellers want low prices
check.why: Buyers buy more when prices fall. Sellers offer more when prices rise. They go opposite ways.

sections.title: Why Prices Go Up and Down

lessons.title: When Many Want and Few Are for Sale
lessons.mainIdea: When many people want something and only a few are for sale, the price goes up.
reading: A new toy comes out before a holiday. A store gets 20 of them. But 100 families want one. There are not enough toys for everyone. This is called a *shortage*. More people want to buy than there are items to sell.

In a shortage, buyers compete for the few items. Some will pay more to be sure they get one. Sellers notice the long lines. So the price goes up. As the price rises, some buyers decide it costs too much. The line gets shorter.

The price keeps rising until the number people want matches the number for sale. So the rule is simple. High demand and low supply push the price up. This is why concert tickets for a famous singer can cost a lot.

words.d: when people want to buy more of something than sellers have for sale
the amount of money a buyer pays for a good or service

look.title: The Last Snow Shovels
look.text: A big snowstorm is coming to Chicago tomorrow. The hardware store has 15 snow shovels left. Dozens of people come in to buy one. Yesterday, only two people wanted a shovel.
look.prompt: Is this a shortage? What might happen to the price of a snow shovel, and why?

check.q: A store has 30 video games. 90 people want to buy one. What is this called?
check.why: More people want to buy than there are items for sale. That is a shortage.

check.q: In a shortage, what usually happens to the price?
check.why: Buyers compete for the few items, so sellers can raise the price.

check.q: Why does a rising price make a shortage smaller?
choices: Some buyers decide the item costs too much
check.why: As the price goes up, fewer people want to buy. The number wanted gets closer to the number for sale.

lessons.title: When There Is Too Much
lessons.mainIdea: When there is more for sale than people want, the price goes down.
reading: A farm stand picks 200 pumpkins in October. At $8 each, only 80 people buy one. When November comes, 120 pumpkins are left. There are more pumpkins for sale than people want. This is called a *surplus*.

In a surplus, sellers have a problem. Pumpkins will rot if nobody buys them. So the farmer lowers the price. The sign now says $3 each. At the lower price, more people decide to buy. Some buy two pumpkins to make pie.
The price keeps falling until the pumpkins sell. So this is the other half of the rule. Low demand and high supply push the price down. That is why stores hold sales on winter coats in the spring.

words.d: when sellers have more of something for sale than people want to buy
a time when a seller lowers the price to sell more

look.title: Too Many Sunglasses
look.text: A store ordered 500 pairs of sunglasses for the summer. It was a rainy summer. By August, the store still has 300 pairs on the shelf. The store needs the space for school supplies.
look.prompt: Is this a shortage or a surplus? What would you do with the price if you ran the store?

check.q: A farm stand has 200 pumpkins and sells 80. How many are left?
check.why: 200 - 80 = 120 pumpkins are left. That leftover is a surplus.

check.q: A store has more winter coats than people want in April. What will the store most likely do?
choices: Keep the price the same all year
check.why: In a surplus, sellers lower the price so more people will buy.

check.q: Which sentence describes a surplus?
choices: Every item sells in one hour
50 bikes are for sale but only 10 people want one
check.why: A surplus means more for sale than people want. 50 bikes and only 10 buyers is a surplus.

lessons.title: A Hot Day and a Cold Day
lessons.mainIdea: When something changes how much people want, like the weather, the price can change too.
reading: Sam runs a lemonade stand. On a hot Saturday, 60 people want lemonade at 50 cents a cup. Sam has only 40 cups. That is a shortage, so Sam raises his price to 75 cents. Now about 40 people want a cup, and he sells out.

On a cold, rainy Sunday, only 15 people want lemonade at 50 cents. Sam still has 40 cups. That is a surplus. So Sam lowers the price to 25 cents. More people stop to buy. The weather changed the demand, and the price followed.

Many things can change demand. The weather, a holiday, a new fad or more people in town can all change how much people want. When demand goes up, the price tends to rise. When demand goes down, the price tends to fall.

words.d: how much of a good people are willing and able to buy at each price
when people want to buy more of something than sellers have for sale
when sellers have more of something for sale than people want to buy

look.title: Sam's Lemonade at 50 Cents
look.prompt: Sam has 40 cups each day. On which days is there a shortage? A surplus?

check.q: Sam has 40 cups. On the hot Saturday, 60 people want one. How many people cannot get a cup at 50 cents?
check.why: 60 people want a cup but only 40 cups exist. 60 - 40 = 20 people are left out.

check.q: A new movie makes a toy very popular. What will likely happen to the toy's price?
check.why: More people want the toy, so demand goes up. Higher demand tends to push the price up.

check.q: On the rainy Sunday, why did Sam lower his price?
choices: He had more cups than people wanted
check.why: Only 15 people wanted lemonade but Sam had 40 cups. In a surplus, a lower price helps sell more.

lessons.title: More Sellers, Better Deals
lessons.mainIdea: Competition among sellers leads to lower prices, better quality and better service for buyers.
reading: Jada was the only lemonade stand on Elm Street. She could charge 75 cents a cup. Then Leo opened a stand across the street for 60 cents. Now buyers had a choice. Jada lowered her price to 55 cents and added ice.

When sellers try to win the same buyers, that is *competition*. Each seller wants buyers to pick them. So they lower prices, make better products or give friendlier service. The buyers win. They get more for their money.

Competition also pushes sellers to try new ideas. A bakery might add a new flavor. A shop might stay open later. When there is only one seller, that seller has less reason to improve. Buyers have nowhere else to go.

words.d: when sellers try to win the same buyers with better prices, quality or service
a person who buys and uses goods and services

look.title: Adam Smith on Buyers and Sellers
look.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776
look.prompt: Benevolence means kindness. Smith says the baker sells bread to help himself. How does that still help you get dinner?

check.q: Jada charged 75 cents. Leo opened a stand for 60 cents. Jada changed to 55 cents. How much less does a cup cost at Jada's now?
check.why: 75 cents - 55 cents = 20 cents less than before.

check.q: A town has one pizza shop. A second pizza shop opens. What will likely happen?
choices: Shops try to offer better deals
check.why: Competition makes sellers try to win buyers with better prices, quality or service.

check.q: Who gains the most from competition among sellers?
check.why: Buyers get lower prices, better goods and more choices when sellers compete.

lessons.title: A Price Is a Signal
lessons.mainIdea: A price is a signal that tells buyers and sellers what to do.
reading: A traffic light sends a signal. Green means go. Red means stop. Prices send signals too. When the price of strawberries is high, it tells farmers, grow more strawberries. It tells buyers, maybe buy blueberries this week.

A high price is a *signal* that something is scarce. Sellers see a chance to earn more, so they make more. Buyers see a reason to buy less or find a *substitute*. A substitute is something you can use instead, like apple juice instead of orange juice.

A low price sends the opposite signal. It tells sellers to make less and tells buyers it is a good time to buy. Nobody has to give orders. Millions of people read prices and make their own choices. Together, those choices move goods where people want them.

words.d: information that tells people what to do; a price signals how scarce something is
a good you can use instead of another, like apple juice instead of orange juice

look.title: Tracing a Price Signal
look.text: Orange juice suddenly costs twice as much after a bad freeze hurts orange trees. Families at the store stand in front of the juice aisle and look at the prices.
look.prompt: What does the high price tell shoppers to do? What does it tell orange growers in other places to do?

check.q: The price of eggs goes way up. What signal does this send to farmers?
check.why: A high price signals that sellers can earn more, so they want to produce more.

check.q: Beef costs a lot this week, so the Garcia family buys chicken instead. What is chicken here?
check.why: A substitute is something you use instead of another good. Chicken took the place of beef.

check.q: What does a low price usually tell sellers?
check.why: A low price signals that there is plenty. Sellers earn less, so they make less.

lessons.title: Where the Price Settles
lessons.mainIdea: The market price settles where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.
reading: Put buyers and sellers together. At $2 a muffin, kids want 10 but Jada bakes 35. That is a surplus, so the price falls. At 50 cents, kids want 40 but Jada bakes only 10. That is a shortage, so the price rises.

At $1, kids want 20 muffins and Jada bakes 20. Nothing is left over, and nobody is left out. This is the *market price*. Economists call it the *equilibrium* price. It is where the amount people want equals the amount for sale.

The market price can move. If a hot day or a new fad raises demand, the price rises to a new level. If more sellers join, supply rises and the price falls. Prices keep adjusting as buyers and sellers change their plans.

words.d: the price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer
the point where the amount people want to buy equals the amount for sale

look.title: Find the Muffin Price
look.text: At $2.00 kids want 10 muffins and Jada bakes 35. At $1.50 kids want 14 and Jada bakes 28. At $1.00 kids want 20 and Jada bakes 20. At $0.50 kids want 40 and Jada bakes 10. (Made-up example.)
look.prompt: At which price is there no shortage and no surplus? How do you know?

check.q: At $1.50, kids want 14 muffins and Jada bakes 28. How many muffins are left over?
check.why: 28 baked - 14 wanted = 14 muffins left over. That is a surplus.

check.q: What is true at the market price?
choices: The amount wanted equals the amount for sale
check.why: At the market price, or equilibrium, the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.

check.q: Five new muffin bakers join the school sale. What will likely happen to the market price?
check.why: More sellers means more supply. More supply tends to push the price down.

review.q: Which of these is a market?
choices: An online shop where people buy books
A river flowing to a lake
review.why: A market is any place or way buyers and sellers meet to trade.

review.q: The price of apples drops from $2 a pound to $1 a pound. What will buyers most likely do?
review.why: The law of demand: when the price goes down, people buy more.

review.q: A toy maker can now sell each toy for $10 instead of $6. What will the toy maker most likely do?
review.why: The law of supply: when the price goes up, sellers offer more.

review.q: A store has 10 tickets and 50 people want them. What is this, and what happens to the price?
review.why: More people want tickets than there are for sale. That is a shortage, so the price rises.

review.q: A candy store has 200 leftover chocolate hearts after Valentine's Day. What will likely happen?
review.why: This is a surplus. Sellers lower the price to sell what is left.

review.q: A second ice cream truck starts driving through the neighborhood. How does this help buyers?
choices: The trucks compete with better prices or service
review.why: Competition pushes sellers to offer lower prices, better quality or better service.

review.q: A cup of lemonade rises from 50 cents to 75 cents. How much did the price go up?
At 40 cents, kids want 30 stickers and a seller offers 30. What is 40 cents?
review.why: The amount wanted equals the amount for sale, so 40 cents is the market price, or equilibrium.
